Tischler and Piet Maes The citation for this ICTV Report chapter is the summary published as: Bradfute, S. B., Calisher, C. H., Klempa, B., Klingström, J., Kuhn, J. H., Laenen, L., Tischler, N. D., & Maes, P. (2024). ICTV Virus Taxonomy Profile: Hantaviridae 2024, Journal of General Virology 105, 001975 Corresponding author: Piet Maes ( [email protected] ) Edited by: Holly Hughes and Evelien Adriaenssens Posted: March 2024, updated June 2024 Summary Hantaviridae is a family for negative-sense RNA viruses with genomes of about 10.5–14.6 kb (Table 1 Hantaviridae ). The family includes eight genera ( Actinovirus and Percilovirus (subfamily Actantavirinae ), Agnathovirus (subfamily Agantavirinae ), Loanvirus , Mobatvirus , Orthohantavirus and Thottimvirus (subfamily Mammantavirinae ), and Reptillovirus (subfamily Repantavirinae ). These viruses are maintained in and/or transmitted by small mammals, but also by fish and reptiles. Several orthohantaviruses can infect humans, causing mild, severe, and sometimes-fatal diseases. Hantavirids produce enveloped virions containing three single-stranded RNA segments with open reading frames (ORFs) that encode a nucleoprotein (N), a glycoprotein precursor (GPC), and large (L) protein containing an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain. Table 1 Hantaviridae. Characteristics of members of the family Hantaviridae. Characteristic Description* Example Hantaan virus (S segment: M14626; M segment: M14627; L segment: X55901), species Orthohantavirus hantanense Virion Enveloped, pleomorphic virions 80–160 nm in diameter with heterodimeric surface spikes Genome Three single-stranded RNA molecules (segments): small (S; 1.0–3.0 kb), medium (M; 3.4–4.8 kb), and large (L; 5.3–6.8 kb) Replication Ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes containing anti-genomic RNA serve as coding templates for synthesis of genomic RNA Translation Proteins are produced from capped and non-polyadenylated mRNAs. The 5′-cap structure is obtained via cap-snatching from cellular mRNAs Host range Fish (actinoviruses, agnathoviruses, perciloviruses), mammals (orthohantaviruses), and reptiles (reptilloviruses) Taxonomy Realm Riboviria , kingdom Orthornavirae , phylum Negarnaviricota , class Bunyaviricetes , order Elliovirales ; the family includes four subfamilies, eight genera, and 55 species * mostly based on experiments with mammalian orthohantaviruses Viruses assigned to each of the seven genera form genus-specifc monophyletic clades based on phylogenetic analysis of concatenated L protein/RdRP, glycoprotein and N sequences. Viruses from all seven genera share one or more of the following characteristics: (i) enveloped pleomorphic virions; (ii) tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genome without polyadenylated tracts at the 3′-end; (iii) genomic sequence complementarity at the 5′- and 3′-ends; and (iv) capped but not polyadenylated virus mRNAs ( Maes et al., 2004 ). Piscine Hosts Genus Actinovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian (percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) fish. Genus Agnathovirus . Viruses in this genus infect agnathan (myxinid) fish. Genus Percilovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian ( gobiid, lophiid ) fish. Mammalian Hosts Genus Loanvirus. Viruses in this genus infect rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly nycterid bats and possibly murid rodents. Genus Mobatvirus. Viruses in this genus infect emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid and possibly molossid, and vespertillionid bats and soricid and talpid eulipotyphla. Genus Orthohantavirus. Viruses assigned to this genus infect soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Genus Thottimvirus. Viruses in this genus infect soricid and possibly talpid eulipotyphla. Reptilian Hosts Genus Reptillovirus . Viruses in this genus infect gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles. Virion Morphology Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Physicochemical and physical properties Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Nucleic acid Hantavirids have tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genomes (S, M, and L segments). The viral mRNAs are not polyadenylated and contain a 5′-methylated cap and several non-templated nucleotides at the 5′-end that are derived from host cell mRNAs via cap snatching ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Further information is only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Proteins Hantavirids typically express three structural proteins. The most abundant structural protein in a hantavirion is N, which encapsidates the hantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , are produced from GPC and mediate entry of hantavirions ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Spiropoulou 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Lipids Not reported but are likely derived from the Golgi apparatus and/or the host cell plasma membrane and therefore likely composed of phospholipids, glycolipids, fatty acids, and sterols. Carbohydrates Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Genome organization and replication S RNA encodes N and in some viruses NSs ( Jääskeläinen et al., 2007 , Vera-Otarola et al., 2012 ), M RNA encodes GPC, and the L RNA encodes L with its RdRP, helicase, and endonuclease domains ( Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 ) (Figure 1 Hantaviridae ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Figure 1 Hantaviridae . Genome organization of representative hantaviruses. The 5′- and 3′- ends of all segments are complementary at their termini, likely promoting the formation of panhandle RNP complexes within the virion . GPC , glycoprotein precursor gene; L , large (protein) gene; N , nucleoprotein gene. Biology Hantavirids have been found in actinopterygian (gobiid, lophiid, percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) and agnathan (myxinid) fish; in emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid, rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly molossid and nycterid bats; in soricid and talpid eulipotyphla; in muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents; in gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles; and potentially in coleopteran and plectopteran insects (see genus pages for details). Only orthohantaviruses are known to cause diseases (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Antigenicity Systematic antigenicity studies have only been reported for orthohantaviruses (see Orthohantavirus genus page). species demarcation criteria The availability of at least coding-complete sequences of all three genome segments may be sufficient for hantavirid classification in the absence of a cultured isolate. Demarcation of genera is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Hantaviridae: current classification and future perspectives, Viruses, 11, 9, e0788">Laenen et al., 2019 ). DEmARC analysis gave a frequency distribution of Pairwise Evolutionary Distance (PED) values of which the threshold of 0.1 gave an optimal clustering cost of zero and is used as the hantavirid species demarcation criterium. Genera are demarked by a PED-value threshold of 0.95 and subfamilies are demarcated based on their distinct clustering in a Bayesian maximum clade credibility tree and a PED-value threshold of 3.5. Relationships within the family Phylogenetic relationships across the family have been estimated using Bayesian maximum clade credibility trees generated from complete N, GPC, and L amino-acid sequences; similar topologies are obtained with concatenated N and GPC sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Figure 2 Hantaviridae . Maximum likelihood phylogenetic tree inferred using IQ-TREE. The tree was constructed based on 53 concatenated S and M segment (amino acid) sequences using the LG+R9 model of sequence evolution. Branch lengths represent the estimated number of substitutions per site. Bootstrap support values (>70%) are indicated at nodes, reflecting the degree of confidence in the branching pattern. Relationships with other taxa Hantavirids are closely related to bunyaviral crulivirids, fimovirids, peribunyavirids, phasmavirids, tulasvirids, and tospovirids ( Wolf et al., 2018 , Herath et al., 2020 ). Using the Master Species List Using the Virus Metadata Resource Using the Find the Species tool Using the ICTV Report Webinar Webinar on Virus Taxonomy Webinar on Finding Information GitHub Repository Zenodo Repository Email ICTV Help ‏‏‎ ‎ ICTV Report Book: Hantaviridae Family: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Actantavirinae Genus: Actinovirus Genus: Percilovirus Subfamily: Agantavirinae Genus: Agnathovirus Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Loanvirus Genus: Mobatvirus Genus: Orthohantavirus Genus: Thottimvirus Subfamily: Repantavirinae Genus: Reptillovirus Authors: Hantaviridae Citation: Hantaviridae References: Hantaviridae Resources: Hantaviridae Species List: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Orthohantavirus Distinguishing features Sixty different viruses are classified in the genus Orthohantavius. These viruses typically infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease in humans ( Schmaljohn and Hjelle 1997 , Jonsson et al., 2010 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 , Vial et al., 2023 ). Virion Morphology Orthohantavirions are pleomorphic in shape, mostly spherical of 80–160 nm in diameter ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ), and surrounded by a membrane envelope that is decorated with glycoprotein (GP) spikes composed of G N and G C subunits (Figure 1 Orthohantavirus ). The virion envelope is 5 nm thick and is decorated with square shaped spikes, consisting of tetrameric G N -G C heterodimers, which protrude 10 nM from the membrane forming a surface lattice of local symmetry interrupted by empty membrane spots ( Hung et al., 1983 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Parvate et al., 2019 , Serris et al., 2020 , Guardado-Calvo and Rey 2021 ). Isolated ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes are composed of individual segment genomic RNA encapsidated by nucleoprotein (N) ( Tao et al., 1987 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Hepojoki et al., 2012 , Guo et al., 2016 , Arragain et al., 2019 ). Virions assemble and bud from the Golgi complex or cell surface membranes, depending on the virus ( Goldsmith et al., 1995 , Parvate et al., 2019 ). Figure 1 Orthohantavirus. A, B) Electron micrographs of Tula virus particles adapted from ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ). C) Schematic illustration of an orthohantavirus particle. Shown is a spherical and enveloped (grey) particle with glycoprotein spikes (G N yellow, G C blue) inserted in a bilaminar lipid envelope. The S (small), M (medium), and L (large) RNP (ribonucleoprotein) complexes inside the particle consist of N (nucleoprotein, green) and L (large protein, pink). ViralZone image reproduced courtesy of SwissBioPics. Physicochemical and physical properties Virion buoyant densities in sucrose and CsCl are 1.15–1.18 ( White et al., 1982 ) and 1.20–1.21 g cm −3 , respectively ( Schmaljohn et al., 1983 ). Virions are sensitive to chemical inactivation with, for instance, methanol, paraformaldehyde, acetone/methanol, N -ethylmaleimide or detergents, as well as physical methods such as heat, gamma irradiation or UV irradiation ( Kraus et al., 2005 , Strandin et al., 2011 , Elveborg et al., 2022 ). Nucleic acid Orthohantavirus genomes are linear tri-segmented RNA molecules of negative polarity. The genomes are about 11.1–12.3 kb in length (small [S] segment: 1.2–2.1 kb; medium [M] segment: 3.4–3.8 kb; large [L] segment: 6.5–6.6 kb). Proteins Orthohantaviruses typically express three structural proteins (Table 1 Orthohantavirus ). The most abundant structural protein in an orthohantavirion is N, which encapsidates the orthohantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , mediate virion entry. G N and G C and non-structural proteins are encoded as a precursor polyprotein. Table 1 Orthohantavirus . Location and function of orthohantavirus structural proteins. Protein Location, mass, and function Reference Nucleoprotein (N) Structural virion protein (about 48 kD). Oligomerizes and encapsidates orthohantaviral genomic segments and hence component of RNPs. Binds to L and G N ( Mir et al., 2010 , Reuter and Krüger 2018 , Arragain et al., 2019 ) Nonstructural protein (NSs) Non-structural protein encoded by some orhtohantaviruses. Has type I interferon inhibitory activity. May occur as multiple isoforms. ( Vera-Otarola et al., 2020 , Binder et al., 2021 ) Glycoprotein (GP) Structural virion protein consisting of two subunits (G N : about 70-75 kD, G C : about 50-55 kD). Produced via proteolytic cleavage from the genome-encoded precursor GPC. Projects from virion membranes as tetrameric GP spikes composed of G N and G C heterodimers. GP mediates cell- receptor binding; as a class II fusion machine it induces virion-cell membrane fusion and, thereby cell entry. G N binds to N and RNA ( Spiropoulou et al., 2003 , Tischler et al., 2005 , Cifuentes-Muñoz et al., 2014 , Li et al., 2016 , Willensky et al., 2016 , Rissanen et al., 2017 , Zhu et al., 2018 , Bignon et al., 2019 , Sperber et al., 2019 ) Large protein (L) Structural virion protein (246 kD) with RdRP, helicase, and endoribonuclease domains. Component of the RNP inside virions. Binds to N and RNA. Oligomerizes and mediates transcription and replication of viral RNA segments. Mediates cap-snatching for viral mRNA capping. ( Kukkonen et al., 2005 , Cheng et al., 2014 , Rothenberger et al., 2016 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Durieux Trouilleton et al., 2023 ) Genome organization and replication The orthohantavirus genome consists of three negative-sense RNA molecules, termed S (small), M (medium), and L (large) (Figure 2 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 2 Orthohantavirus. Schematic representation of orthohantavirus genome organization. Orthohantavirus genomic segments assume circular forms via non-covalent binding of complementary and highly conserved 3′- and 5′-terminal sequences. Genomic segment reassortment mostly occurs among viruses belonging to the same species but interspecies reassortment likely occurs occasionally ( Klempa 2018 , Petazzi et al., 2021 ). Orthohantavirus infection starts with virion attachment, mediated by G N and G C , to cell-surface attachment factors and entry via the endosomal route ( Shtanko et al., 2014 ) (Figure 3 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 3 Orthohantavirus . Lifecycle of orthohantaviruses. (1) Virion attachment; (2) virion uptake; (3) virion-cell membrane fusion; (4) transcription; (5) translation; (6) replication; (7) virion assembly; and (8) virion egress. After engaging a cellular receptor, protocadherin 1 in the case of American orthohantaviruses, virion-membrane fusion results in early or late endosomal release, depending on the virus, of the virion RNP complex into the cytoplasm in a pH-dependent manner ( Jangra et al., 2018 , Mittler et al., 2019 , Torriani et al., 2019 , Dieterle et al., 2021 ). During primary transcription L generates uncapped antigenomic RNA molecules that are then capped using host cell-derived capped primers (cap snatching). L and S segment-transcribed mRNAs are translated by free ribosomes ( Garcin et al., 1995 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Meier et al., 2021 ). M segment-transcribed mRNA is translated by membrane-bound ribosomes, with the expressed GPC which is likely co-translationally cleaved by cellular proteases to yield G N and G C . The synthesis of the antigenome by L protein serves as a template for genomic RNA replication. Secondary transcription amplifies the synthesis of mRNAs and genome replication. During morphogenesis, G N and G C accumulate in the Golgi apparatus, modified host membranes are acquired, and virions bud into the Golgi. Biology Genus Orthohantavirus includes 38 species for 60 distinct viruses. These viruses and their unclassified, potential relatives, subclinically, and often chronically, infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla, and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents ( Jonsson et al., 2010 , Wu et al., 2018 , Chen et al., 2023 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are overall distributed worldwide, but the individual geographic distribution is dependent on host range. At least some orthohantaviruses may not be as restricted to a particular host as originally thought, but may be carried by animals of multiple hosts ( Goodfellow et al., 2021 , Quizon et al., 2022 , Gu et al., 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease (all in humans) and all disease-causing viruses are rodent-borne. Human infection may occur after inhalation of aerosolized excreta or secreta of infected rodents or direct rodent contact. The two WHO-recognized orthohantavirus-caused diseases are hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), caused by Asian and European viruses (in particular Dobrava virus [DOBV], Hantaan virus [HTNV], Puumala virus [PUUV] and Seoul virus [SEOV]), and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a frequently lethal disease caused by viruses from the Americas (in particular Andes virus [ANDV] and Sin Nombre virus [SNV]) ( Vial et al., 2023 ). The hamster model of wild-type ANDV infection is lethal and largely mimics human HPS ( Hooper et al., 2001 ). After SNV infection in nonhuman primates, some animals develop an HPS-like disease, but cell passage of SNV can result in mutations that render the virus non-pathogenic in this model ( Safronetz et al., 2014 ). Many rodent models result in a chronic, asymptomatic infection, and these have been used in early-stage therapeutic studies ( Strandin et al., 2020 ). However, recent advances have been made in development of an HFRS mouse model using HTNV variants ( Wei et al., 2022 ). Orthohantavirus animal models are reviewed in ( Golden et al., 2015 ). Antigenicity There is considerable serum cross-reactivity between the nucleocapsids of hantavirids, but neutralizing antibodies targeting Gn/Gc are more specific. SNV was first identified as a hantavirid based on cross-reactivity of patient sera with other orthohantavirus antigens ( 1993 ). Similarly, rodents that carried SNV were identified in serosurveys using non-SNV orthohantavirus antigens, since SNV had not been isolated at the time ( Childs et al., 1994 ). Species demarcation criteria Demarcation of species is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Laenen et al., 2019 ). Phylogenetic relationships across the genus have been estimated using maximum likelihood trees generated from complete N, GPC and L amino-acid sequences, and for N and GPC amino-acid sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Hantaviridae ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Hantaviridae (taxid:1980413) VIRION Enveloped, spherical. Diameter from 80 to 120nm. GENOME Segmented Negative-stranded RNA linear genome, L segment is between 6.8 and 12 kb, M segment between 3.2 and 4.9 kb and S segment between 1 and 3 kb. Encodes for four to six proteins. Some hantaviruses also encode a NSs protein on their S segment. GENE EXPRESSION The viral RNA dependent RNA polymerase (L) binds to a promoter on each encapsidated segment, and transcribes the mRNA. These are capped by L protein during synthesis using cap snatching . Transcription is terminated by a strong hairpin sequence at the end of each gene. Puumala virus expressed an additional NSs by leaky scanning in the NS gene. ENZYMES RNA-dependent RNA polymerase L Cap Snatching endonuclease L REPLICATION CYTOPLASMIC Virus attaches to host receptors though Gn-Gc glycoprotein dimer, and is endocytosed into vesicles in the host cell. Fusion of virus membrane with the vesicle membrane; ribonucleocapsid segments are released in the cytoplasm. Transcription , viral mRNAs are capped in the cytoplasm. Replication presumably starts when enough nucleoprotein is present to encapsidate neo-synthetized antigenomes and genomes. The ribonucleocapsids buds at Golgi apparatus, releasing the virion by exocytosis. The hantaviruses (Hantaviridae) ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Back to Andes virus resource There are approximately 92 known viruses in the family Hantaviridae, classified into 52 species. Each species is typically adapted to a specific reservoir host, most commonly rodents, but also bats and moles. With the notable exception of Andes virus, hantaviruses are generally not transmitted from person to person. Based on their geographic distribution, evolutionary relationships, and the diseases they cause in humans, hantaviruses can be broadly divided into three major groups: New World hantaviruses (the Americas) These viruses cause Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a severe respiratory disease. Important examples include Sin Nombre virus and Andes virus. Annual incidence are about 100 cases per year (Andes virus) about 25 cases per year (Sin Nombre virus) Old World hantaviruses (Asia) These viruses are responsible for Hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), which is characterized by fever, hemorrhage, and acute kidney injury. Major examples include Hantaan virus and Seoul virus. Annual incidence: more than 10,000 cases worldwide Old World hantaviruses (Europe) European hantaviruses typically cause a milder form of HFRS known as Nephropathia epidemica (NE). The main causative agents are Puumala virus and Dobrava-Belgrade virus. Annual incidence: more than 1,000 cases Together, these viruses represent an important and diverse group of zoonotic pathogens that can cause severe disease following accidental transmission from their natural animal hosts to humans.

papers.title: Hantaan virus polymerase has an in vitro Terminal Nucleotidyl Transferase activity that is conserved across the Bunyaviricetes class
papers.abstract: Bunyaviricetes is a class of segmented negative strand RNA viruses (sNSV) that includes causative agents of severe zoonotic diseases resulting in hemorrhagic fever in humans and livestock. Hantaan virus (HTNV), family Hantaviridae, is an example of life-threatening bunyavirus transmitted by rodents which leads to Hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in humans. Infection relies on the replication and transcription of their tripartite genomes through multifunctional RNA-dependent RNA polymerases (RdRp) in the context of ribonucleoproteins (RNPs) made of one viral RNA fragment, one RdRp and multiple copies of viral nucleoproteins. The RdRp, also known as L protein, performs replication by de novo initiation through a prime-and-realign mechanism while transcription initiates through a cap snatching mechanism, that engages a cap-binding domain and an endonuclease (EN) domain present in the L protein C and N terminal regions, respectively. In this work we show that HTNV L protein has a terminal nucleotidyl transferase (TNTase) activity over double-stranded RNA substrates (dsRNA) in vitro. We show that the TNTase activity is also present in other bunyaviral L proteins by comparing HTNV L protein activity with La Crosse (LACV, family Orthobunyaviridae) and Crimean Congo Hemorrhagic Fever Virus (CCHFV, family Nairoviridae) L proteins. Our results show that TNTase activity appears to be a general feature of Bunyaviruses and report the differences on substrate and nucleotide specificity for each family of virus.

analysis.background: Bunyaviricetes are segmented negative‑strand RNA viruses that cause severe zoonotic hemorrhagic fevers (A1); Hantaan virus, a rodent‑borne hantavirus, leads to hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in humans (A2).

papers.title: Hantaviruses at an inflection point: scientific evidence, spillover risk, and One Health approach
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses are zoonotic RNA viruses that cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome and are primarily maintained in rodent reservoirs. Transmission to humans occurs mainly by inhalation of aerosolized excreta from infected rodents, but Andes virus uniquely shows documented limited person-to-person spread with important clinical and public-health implications. Environmental change, urbanization, and global mobility have broadened hantavirus geographic risk and contributed to recent multi-country clusters, including expedition cruise-ship–associated events that highlighted preparedness gaps. This review synthesizes current knowledge on hantavirus taxonomy, molecular biology, transmission pathways, host reservoirs, pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnostics, and management, and it critically assesses advances in molecular surveillance, phylogenetics, antiviral research, and emerging nanobiotechnological approaches. I operationalize a One Health framework into concrete prevention and control actions, integrated human–animal–environment surveillance, targeted rodent reservoir monitoring and control, environmental sampling, and formal intersectoral coordination mechanisms, and I map epidemiologic findings to prioritized, group-specific public-health interventions. Finally, I identify current controversies and knowledge gaps (reservoir competence, surveillance sensitivity, and limits of predictive models), and propose a research and policy agenda to strengthen global preparedness for high-consequence hantavirus events.

papers.title: Hantavirus as a persistent zoonotic risk: epidemiology and current pharmacological management
papers.abstract: Background Hantaviruses are emerging rodent-borne zoonotic viruses that continue to pose a public health concern despite their relatively low incidence in humans. The 2026 Andes virus outbreak linked to the MV Hondius cruise ship renewed international attention on these pathogens, highlighting unresolved questions regarding transmission dynamics, vulnerable populations, and global preparedness. This review provides an updated critical appraisal of recent advances in hantavirus epidemiology, emerging therapeutic strategies, and public health challenges, with particular emphasis on the 2026 Andes virus outbreak, companion animals, and solid organ transplant recipients. Methods A review of the recent literature was performed, focusing on zoonotic transmission, the role of companion animals, current and emerging therapeutic strategies, infections in immunocompromised and solid-organ transplant recipients, and the implications of the 2026 international outbreak. Results Although the sentinel hypothesis remains plausible, companion animals are not natural reservoirs, and preliminary evidence suggests that their exposure may reflect local hantavirus circulation, while pet rats have emerged as an important source of Seoul orthohantavirus infection. Therapeutic options remain limited: supportive care is the standard of treatment, and ribavirin shows benefit only in early hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome. Emerging immunotherapeutic approaches, including neutralizing monoclonal antibodies and host-directed therapies, show promising preclinical results but still lack robust clinical validation. In immunocompromised patients, particularly solid-organ transplant recipients, hantavirus infection may mimic graft rejection or present with atypical, potentially fatal manifestations, posing diagnostic challenges. The 2026 MV Hondius outbreak reinforced the need for heightened surveillance, rapid diagnosis, and coordinated international response, while confirming that sustained human-to-human transmission remains exceptional. Conclusion Recent evidence broadens the clinical and public health relevance of hantaviruses beyond their traditional framing as rodent-borne zoonoses. Advances in targeted therapeutics, integrated surveillance, and One Health preparedness will be pivotal to improving outbreak preparedness and accelerating the development of effective preventive and therapeutic strategies.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses remain a public‑health concern despite low human incidence, prompting renewed review after the 2026 Andes virus outbreak on the MV Hondius cruise ship.
analysis.main_directions: The review focuses on transmission dynamics, vulnerable groups (companion‑animal contacts, solid‑organ transplant recipients), current and emerging therapeutics, and One Health preparedness highlighted by the recent outbreak.
analysis.current_state: Supportive care is the mainstay of treatment; ribavirin benefits early hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, while monoclonal antibodies and host‑directed therapies show promise in preclinical studies but lack clinical validation.
analysis.gaps: Companion animals are not natural reservoirs, yet their exposure may indicate local circulation, and evidence on pet‑rat transmission of Seoul orthohantavirus remains preliminary.
analysis.future_research: Priorities include validating immunotherapeutics in clinical trials, expanding integrated surveillance across wildlife, pets, and humans, and developing targeted therapies and preventive measures within a One Health framework.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses pose ongoing zoonotic risk, highlighted by the 2026 Andes virus cruise‑ship outbreak. Main directions: The review examines transmission, at‑risk populations (pets, transplant recipients), therapeutic options, and One Health preparedness. Current state: Care is supportive; ribavirin helps early HFRS, while monoclonal antibodies and host‑directed therapies are preclinical. Gaps: The role of companion animals and pet rats in transmission is uncertain. Future research: Clinical validation of immunotherapies, integrated wildlife‑human surveillance, and development of targeted treatments and preventive strategies are needed.

papers.title: Climate change, rodent ecology, and the rising risk of hantavirus outbreaks: an alarming public health concern
papers.abstract: The Anthropocene era has been characterized by a higher risk of zoonotic viral outbreaks, which often result from a combination of factors, such as climate change, biodiversity loss, land-use patterns, and increased opportunities for human–animal interactions. The current perspective provides an integrated synthesis of how climate change-driven alterations in rodent ecology impact the molecular evolution, transmission dynamics, and emergence of hantaviruses, with an emphasis on the underlying virological mechanisms and their implications for One Health preparedness. Hantaviruses have undergone extensive diversification throughout their evolution and host adaptation and can infect rodents, bats, reptiles, and fish. Rodents serve as the principal natural reservoirs for hantaviruses, with many viral species exhibiting long-term evolutionary associations with specific rodent host species. Climate change has been recognized as one of the key determinants for the emergence of hantavirus outbreaks in different parts of the world. Climate-related factors may facilitate viral amplification through multiple mechanisms, including their impact on evolution, mutation, and reassortment. To conclude, climate change has shaped the ecology, transmission dynamics, and molecular evolution of hantaviruses by altering rodent behavior, their habitats, and the environmental persistence of viral particles. Climate-induced ecological disruption has created opportunities for viral amplification within reservoir hosts and augmented the risk of zoonotic spillover into humans. These insights provide a conceptual framework for anticipating future outbreaks in the context of climate change and support the integration of ecological, virological, and public health surveillance systems. There is an urgent need to ensure that virological preparedness strategies evolve in accordance with changing environmental conditions by strengthening genomic surveillance and integrated One Health frameworks.

papers.title: Multi-omics Reveals Divergent Endothelial Molecular Responses to New and Old World Hantaviruses
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses cause vascular leakage syndromes that vary in clinical manifestation and severity. Although tissue tropism contributes to these differences, both Old and New World hantaviruses infect endothelial cells, where species-specific disease phenotypes remain poorly understood. Here we integrated time-resolved global RNA sequencing, mass spectrometry proteomics, and phosphoproteomics of human endothelial cells infected with New World Andes virus (ANDV) or Old World Hantaan virus (HTNV). Despite equivalent early viral RNA and protein levels, ANDV elicited a stronger innate immune protein response, preceding its restriction while HTNV replication continued. At later stages of infection, HTNV induced downregulation of cytoskeletal and junctional protein phosphorylation, accompanied by visual disruption of cellular actin architecture. Additionally, ANDV induced heightened activity of ERBB-family kinases, whose chemical inhibition by neratinib and afatinib reduced viral replication. Together, these data define species-specific responses in endothelial cells, identify druggable host targets, and reveal mechanisms with relevance to divergent vascular leakage symptomology.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses cause vascular leakage syndromes with variable severity. Methods: Time‑resolved RNA‑seq, proteomics and phosphoproteomics were performed on human endothelial cells infected with Andes virus or Hantaan virus. papers.title_zh: 多组学揭示新世界和旧世界汉坦病毒的内皮分子反应差异

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒es 引起血管渗漏综合征,临床表现和严重程度各异。
analysis_zh.methods: 采用时间分辨的全局RNA测序、质谱蛋白质组学和磷酸蛋白质组学,对感染新世界安第斯病毒(安第斯病毒)或旧世界汉滩病毒(汉滩病毒)的人类内皮细胞进行分析。
analysis_zh.results: 尽管早期病毒RNA和蛋白水平相当,安第斯病毒引发更强的先天免疫蛋白响应并先于其受限出现,而汉滩病毒复制持续;随后,汉滩病毒下调细胞骨架和连接蛋白磷酸化,伴随可见的肌动蛋白破坏;安第斯病毒诱导ERBB家族激酶活性升高,使用neratinib或afatinib进行化学抑制可降低病毒复制。
analysis_zh.contribution: 该数据定义了物种特异性内皮反应,确定了可药物化的ERBB激酶,并揭示了与不同血管渗漏症状相关的机制。
analysis_zh.limitations: 在提供的证据中未报告。

papers.title: Hantavirus Across Travel, Climate, and Clinical Frontiers: A Global Scoping Review of Emerging Risks (1978-2026)
papers.abstract: This scoping review aims to map the available literature on emerging hantavirus risks across three frontiers: travel-related exposure, climatic and environmental drivers, and clinical frontiers (diagnosis, misdiagnosis, and underrecognition). Following the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology, the review will systematically search thirteen databases and platforms for literature published between 1978 and 2026. Ultimately, this research will map the global evidence landscape, identify knowledge gaps, and highlight priorities for surveillance, travel medicine, climate adaptation, and clinical education.

papers.title: Molecular Surveillance and Evolutionary Characterization of Orthohantavirus jejuense in the Republic of Korea, 2019–2025
papers.abstract: Jeju virus (JJUV), a shrew-borne member of Orthohantavirus jejuense, has been detected in geographically separated populations of Crocidura shantungensis in the Republic of Korea (ROK). However, its distribution and evolutionary characteristics remain incompletely defined. From 2019 to 2025, 56 C. shantungensis were collected from 20 sites across the ROK and screened for JJUV RNA. Viral genomic sequences were characterized using next-generation and Sanger sequencing, followed by phylogenetic, evolutionary, selection-pressure, and in silico B-cell epitope analyses. JJUV RNA was detected in 7 of 56 shrews (12.5%) from Gwangju Metropolitan City, Cheorwon, Chuncheon, and Seogwipo. Coding-complete sequences of all three genomic segments were obtained from three variants, including two from Gwangju, providing genome-resolved evidence of JJUV circulation in the southern mainland. Phylogenetic analyses revealed clear geographic clustering of O. jejuense variants from the northern mainland, Gwangju, Jeju Island, and Ulleung Island. Estimated evolutionary rates ranged from 3.53 × 10−4 to 13.49 × 10−4 substitutions/site/year. Low ratios of nonsynonymous to synonymous substitution rates across the nucleocapsid protein, glycoproteins Gn and Gc, and RNA-dependent RNA polymerase indicated predominantly purifying selection. Sequence- and structure-based analyses predicted six conserved linear B-cell epitope candidates across O. jejuense. Among these, Y165–K175 in the nucleocapsid protein showed the strongest combined structural support. These findings expand the known geographic and genomic diversity of O. jejuense and provide a framework for continued surveillance and future serological studies of its potential zoonotic relevance.

analysis.background: Jeju virus (JJUV), a shrew‑borne Orthohantavirus jejuense, has been detected in Crocidura shantungensis in the Republic of Korea, but its distribution and evolutionary characteristics remain incompletely defined (A1, A2).
analysis.methods: From 2019–2025, 56 C. shantungensis were collected at 20 sites across the ROK and screened for JJUV RNA (A3, A4); viral genomes were sequenced by next‑generation and Sanger methods and analysed phylogenetically, evolutionarily, for selection pressure, and for in silico B‑cell epitopes (A5).
analysis.results: JJUV RNA was found in 7/56 shrews (12.5%) from four locations (A6); coding‑complete sequences of all three segments were obtained from three variants, including two from Gwangju (A7); phylogeny showed clear geographic clustering of variants from the northern mainland, Gwangju, Jeju Island, and Ulleung Island (A8, A9); evolutionary rates were 3.53 × 10⁻⁴–13.49 × 10⁻⁴ substitutions/site/year (A10); low dN/dS ratios indicated predominant purifying selection across key proteins (A11); six conserved linear B‑cell epitope candidates were predicted, with Y165–K175 in the nucleocapsid protein having the strongest structural support (A12, A13).
analysis.contribution: The study expands the known geographic and genomic diversity of O. jejuense (A14) and provides a framework for continued surveillance and future serological investigations of its potential zoonotic relevance (A15).
analysis.limitations: Only an abstract is available, limiting detail on sample handling, statistical analyses, and broader epidemiological context (A3).

analysis.summary_en: Background: Jeju virus, a shrew‑borne Orthohantavirus jejuense, is known in Korea but its distribution and evolution are incompletely defined. Methods: From 2019–2025, 56 Crocidura shantungensis from 20 sites were screened for JJUV RNA; genomes were sequenced (NGS and Sanger) and analysed phylogenetically, evolutionarily, for selection, and for B‑cell epitopes. Results: JJUV RNA was detected in 7/56 shrews (12.5%); complete genomes from three variants revealed geographic clustering, evolutionary rates of 3.53‑13.49 × 10⁻⁴ substitutions/site/year, purifying selection, and six conserved B‑cell epitopes, notably Y165‑K175. Contribution: Findings broaden known geographic/genomic diversity and offer a surveillance framework for potential zoonotic risk. Limitations: Only an abstract is provided, restricting methodological and epidemiological detail.

papers.title: Habitat-Mediated Spillover Risk of Andes Hantavirus in Oligoryzomys longicaudatus: A Mechanistic Eco-Epidemiological Model
papers.abstract: Andes hantavirus (ANDV) is a rodent-borne orthohantavirus associated with hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome in southern South America. Its maintenance and spillover risk depend on the ecology of its principal reservoir, Oligoryzomys longicaudatus, and on environmental changes that alter habitat availability, host abundance, and human–rodent interfaces. We developed a mechanistic eco-epidemiological model that couples effective habitat cover to an SIR framework for ANDV transmission in O. longicaudatus. Habitat degradation and compensatory restoration modify rodent carrying capacity, natality, and the force of infection, which depends on infected host load relative to instantaneous ecological capacity. We derived the habitat equilibrium, the basic reproduction number R0, and the time-dependent effective reproduction number Re(t) and evaluated infection-burden and threshold indicators across degradation-restoration scenarios. The analysis shows that R0 is independent of equilibrium habitat cover because susceptible abundance scales with carrying capacity at the disease-free equilibrium. In contrast, Re(t), cumulative incidence, and infected load depend on transient habitat-mediated crowding. Restoration increases reservoir abundance and absolute infection burden, whereas degradation can reduce abundance while increasing crowding-driven transmission pressure and prolonging supercritical windows. These results identify ecological conditions under which habitat change may intensify reservoir infection pressure and guide One Health surveillance at human–rodent interfaces.

Habitat degradation and compensatory restoration modify rodent carrying capacity, natality, and the force of infection, which depends on infected host load relative to instantaneous ecological capacity. We derived the habitat equilibrium, the basic reproduction number R0, and the time-dependent effective reproduction number Re(t) and evaluated infection-burden and threshold indicators across degradation-restoration scenarios. The analysis shows that R0 is independent of equilibrium habitat cover because susceptible abundance scales with carrying capacity at the disease-free equilibrium. In contrast, Re(t), cumulative incidence, and infected load depend on transient habitat-mediated crowding. Restoration increases reservoir abundance and absolute infection burden, whereas degradation can reduce abundance while increasing crowding-driven transmission pressure and prolonging supercritical windows. These results identify ecological conditions under which habitat change may intensify reservoir infection pressure and guide One Health surveillance at human–rodent interfaces.

papers.full_text: Letters to the Editor 1 Research Letter Hantavirus Infection as a Mimic of Rheumatic Disease: A Selective Diagnostic Approach To the Editor: Recent public health alerts have renewed attention to hantavirus infection, an uncommon but potentially severe zoonosis.1,2 For rheumatologists, its relevance is selective but clinically important in compatible contexts. Hantavirus infection may initially present as an acute febrile inflammatory syndrome with arthritis, arthralgia, or myalgia, variably accompanied by thrombocytopenia, endothelial dysfunction, and renal or pulmonary involvement.3 In patients referred for suspected rheumatic disease, this constellation of signs and symptoms may overlap with inflammatory arthritis, systemic autoimmune disease, immune-mediated renal disease, or vasculitis. The central issue is a diagnostic one: Hantavirus may behave as an infectious mimic of rheumatic disease while the diagnostic evaluation is still ongoing, and treatment decisions may have substantial consequences. Hantavirus should not be considered on the basis of isolated fever or musculoskeletal symptoms alone. Rather, it should enter the rheumatology differential when fever and musculoskeletal manifestations occur together with thrombocytopenia and renal, urinary, pulmonary, capillary leak, or hemorrhagic features, especially when epidemiologic exposure is compatible. Clinically, this phenotype may resemble selected rheumatic presentations, including systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)–associated vasculitis, antiglomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) disease, adult-onset Still disease, inflammatory myopathy, infection-triggered arthritis, or undifferentiated systemic autoimmune disease. Relevant exposures include contact with rodents or rodent-contaminated environments, occupational or domestic exposure in rural or peridomestic settings, recent travel to endemic areas, or exposure associated with an epidemiologically linked hantavirus cluster.3 The epidemiologic pattern is geographically structured. Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is encountered mainly across Europe and Asia, whereas hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) is recognized chiefly in the Americas, with the distribution of individual orthohantaviruses determined by the ecology of their reservoir hosts.3 To date, limited ­ person-to-person transmission has been documented only for Andes virus, a hantavirus endemic to South America.3 The published literature, although limited, illustrates several diagnostic challenges relevant to rheumatology. Musculoskeletal involvement is usually nonspecific; arthralgia and myalgia may accompany HFRS and, in some adults, may be sufficiently prominent to resemble an early inflammatory presentation.4 Thrombocytopenia, renal dysfunction, proteinuria, hema- turia, and hypocomplementemia may prompt consideration of systemic autoimmune or immune-mediated renal disease, including SLE, vasculitis, immune-mediated nephritis, and anti-GBM disease, thereby increasing the risk of diagnostic misclassification. Hantavirus-induced acute kidney injury may mimic immune-mediated glomerular disease, including anti-GBM disease or lupus nephritis, before serologic confirma- tion clarifies the diagnosis.5,6 Vasculitis-like presentations require particular caution. A recent report described myeloperoxidase (MPO)-ANCA– positive pauci-immune small vessel vasculitis with progressive renal dysfunction during acute hantavirus infection.7 This obser- vation establishes a temporal and clinical association but does not demonstrate causation. Earlier serologic data also argue against a frequent relationship. Among 191 patients with estab- lished systemic vasculitides, including granulomatosis with poly- angiitis, microscopic polyangiitis, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and giant cell arteritis, no hantavirus-specific antibodies were detected.8 These findings therefore support diag- nostic vigilance rather than a causal interpretation, particularly when infection-related organ injury and primary autoimmune vasculitis share clinical, serological, or histopathological features. SARS-CoV-2 infection may offer a useful clinical reference for rheumatologists when considering the interface between viral infection and rheumatic disease. Both SARS-CoV-2 and hantaviruses are RNA viruses capable of eliciting prominent systemic inflammatory responses and, in selected cases, arthritis or vasculitis-like manifestations that may resemble ­ immune-mediated disease.3,9,10 Experience with coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) has heightened awareness that viral infections may both mimic and intersect with rheumatic phenotypes. Hantavirus infection may be viewed within this same diagnostic framework, although the underlying biology and clinical syndromes are distinct. From a clinical perspective, severe hantavirus disease, particularly HCPS, may progress rapidly to fulminant cardiopulmonary failure, with case fatality rates reaching up to 50% in the Americas.2,3 Accordingly, hantavirus testing should be guided by the overall clinical and epidemiologic pattern rather than used routinely in rheumatology. Serologic testing may be appropriate when fever and musculoskeletal symptoms coexist with throm- bocytopenia, renal or pulmonary involvement, and a compatible exposure history; reverse transcription PCR can be considered in selected settings according to disease timing, severity, and local laboratory availability. Testing is most useful while the differen- tial diagnosis remains unresolved, particularly before substantial immunomodulatory treatment is initiated. The Figure summa- rizes this selective approach. The central practical implication is selective case recognition rather than routine screening. During periods of increased hanta- virus activity or recognized outbreaks, testing should be reserved for patients in whom the clinical phenotype and exposure history are concordant. Such an approach may reduce premature diagnostic closure, help distinguish infection-related endothelial The Journal of Rheumatology 2026;xx:xxxx doi:10.3899/jrheum.2026-0485 First Release September 15 2026 © 2026 The Journal of Rheumatology 2 The Journal of Rheumatology injury from primary rheumatic disease, and support more accu- rate classification of acute febrile inflammatory presentations. In selected cases, distinguishing infection-related inflammatory presentations, including hantavirus-associated disease, from primary rheumatic disease may also affect the timing or appro- priateness of immunomodulatory therapy. Among 191 patients with estab- lished systemic vasculitides, including granulomatosis with poly- angiitis, microscopic polyangiitis, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and giant cell arteritis, no hantavirus-specific antibodies were detected.8 These findings therefore support diag- nostic vigilance rather than a causal interpretation, particularly when infection-related organ injury and primary autoimmune vasculitis share clinical, serological, or histopathological features. SARS-CoV-2 infection may offer a useful clinical reference for rheumatologists when considering the interface between viral infection and rheumatic disease. Both SARS-CoV-2 and hantaviruses are RNA viruses capable of eliciting prominent systemic inflammatory responses and, in selected cases, arthritis or vasculitis-like manifestations that may resemble ­ immune-mediated disease.3,9,10 Experience with coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) has heightened awareness that viral infections may both mimic and intersect with rheumatic phenotypes. Hantavirus infection may be viewed within this same diagnostic framework, although the underlying biology and clinical syndromes are distinct. From a clinical perspective, severe hantavirus disease, particularly HCPS, may progress rapidly to fulminant cardiopulmonary failure, with case fatality rates reaching up to 50% in the Americas.2,3 Accordingly, hantavirus testing should be guided by the overall clinical and epidemiologic pattern rather than used routinely in rheumatology. Serologic testing may be appropriate when fever and musculoskeletal symptoms coexist with throm- bocytopenia, renal or pulmonary involvement, and a compatible exposure history; reverse transcription PCR can be considered in selected settings according to disease timing, severity, and local laboratory availability. Testing is most useful while the differen- tial diagnosis remains unresolved, particularly before substantial immunomodulatory treatment is initiated. The Figure summa- rizes this selective approach. The central practical implication is selective case recognition rather than routine screening. During periods of increased hanta- virus activity or recognized outbreaks, testing should be reserved for patients in whom the clinical phenotype and exposure history are concordant. In selected cases, distinguishing infection-related inflammatory presentations, including hantavirus-associated disease, from primary rheumatic disease may also affect the timing or appro- priateness of immunomodulatory therapy. papers.full_text: nature health News ‘Desperate rodents’ pose hantavirus risk to humans — boosted by climate change and deforestation Rapid urbanization and changes in rodent behaviour increase the risk of human disease outbreaks, especially in Africa, but experts fear surveillance gaps leave most zoonotic infections undetected. By Tsitsi Bhobo W hen the Andes hantavirus cir­ culated on the M/V Hondius cruise ship, South Africa’s specialist hospitals quickly admitted infected patients and sequenced the virus. But infectious dis­ ease scientists warn that locally derived hanta­ virus strains — including the lethal Sangassou virus — are circulating undetected, hosted by native shrews, rodents and bats1. “At the moment, we believe that hanta­ virus probably is more prevalent [and] widespread than diagnosed in Africa,” says Tulio de Oliveira, Professor at Stellenbosch University, South Africa, and director of the Centre for Epidemic Response and Innova­ tion. Such infections are mainly “self-limited transmission clusters between rodents, other animals and humans,” he tells Nature Health. De Oliveira’s lab is one of a small number across Africa that test for viruses in wild animals, including rodents, bats and non- human primates. Surveillance gap Hantaviruses pose a bigger systematic dan­ ger to Africa’s public health architecture than previously thought, argued de Oliveira and colleagues in a recent article. Limited diag­ nostic and testing capacity and lack of moni­ toring infrastructure, combined with climate change and urbanization, are leading to more zoonotic outbreaks. Africa has a clinical surveillance gap, with viral spillovers probably occurring without being detected by stretched public health authorities. During the current Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Uganda, many of the early infections were suspected to be cases of malaria, leading to delays in the public health response. The DRC has the second highest bur­ den of malaria in the world, leading to tens of thousands of deaths each year. Many other zoonotic infections could be missed. Hillary Young, an ecologist at the University of California Santa Barbara, USA, notes that “we don’t know how big the burden of hanta­ virus is because we haven’t looked for it, really. We don’t have that surveillance.” “One of the acute problems facing Africa is that there is little clinical research into the ecology of hantaviruses, [such as] which specific animals host them,” she says. Such research, including genetics, would “empower scientists to map the interaction between hosts and viruses and calculate the possible harm to humans — in real time,” she adds. With surveillance capacity absent, doctors often report possible hantavirus infections as ‘fever of unknown origin’. “It’s hard, because hantavirus is another one of these diseases that kind of overlaps with lots of other unex­ plained febrile diseases,” says Young. This challenge persists despite South Africa having amongst the best infectious disease genomic surveillance infrastructure in the world. Laboratories across Africa are usually focused on supporting clinical studies in humans, but during outbreaks, resources are diverted to test animals for zoonotic infec­ tions. There are only a small number of such labs across the continent, such as the South Africa National Institute for Communicable Diseases, the Institut Pasteur de Dakar in Senegal and the Uganda Virus Research Unit. These labs act very quickly to develop reagents for new pathogens, test samples and develop metagenomics assays, but the bottleneck leads to inevitable delays, with zoonotic out­ breaks often underdiagnosed for weeks. Urbanization and deforestation Hantavirus spillover in Africa is likely to be linked to loss of biodiversity, rapid urbaniza­ tion and climate change. A recent outbreak of hantaviruses in South America spread beyond rural settings and into urban environments, Hantavirus particles under an electron microscope, with colour enhanced. CREDIT: ALFRED PASIEKA/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/GETTY nature health News possibly because climate variations are lead­ ing to milder and shorter winters in Argentina. Rapid urbanization — widespread across the continent — leads to increased risk, as rats breed in cities where residents regularly interact with wildlife. “We’ll have a bigger pro­ liferation of concentrated rodents,” in Africa’s fast-urbanizing landscapes, says Young, lead­ ing to more zoonotic outbreaks. Young’s research has shown how declines in large wildlife in East Africa were associated with an increase in the prevalence of a rodent- borne bacterium, Bartonella, which can infect humans — providing a link between biodiver­ sity loss and zoonotic disease outbreaks2. Climate change and change of land use in Africa drive rodents to find new breeding zones in human landscapes, warns Young. Rapid expansion of cities across Africa, many without investment in sewerage, creates food and opportunities for rodent species that are already adapted to live alongside humans. This creates the conditions for ‘boom dynamics’, says Young, where rodent popula­ tions increase rapidly. This means periods of explosive, exponential growth for rat popula­ tions followed by often calamitous declines3. “You might get really desperate rodents,” she says, where the animals are “forced into kind of aggressive behaviour. Fighting in rodents can help spread disease among them at higher prevalence.” One Health The genomic surveillance labs in Africa, Latin America and Asia have considerable expertise but fewer resources than their counterparts in high-income countries, says Young. Despite these constraints, they are doing valuable work closest to the regions where zoonotic diseases are most likely to spring up. Africa is taking a lead in shifting the ‘One Health’ model towards building long-term skills, surveillance and diagnostics infrastructure in the global south, the type of capacity that remains resilient through crises. Several African countries, including the DRC and Uganda, have adopted ‘One Health’ frame­ works, an approach pioneered by Rwanda4. But such frameworks need to extend beyond the countryside and integrate with cities in Africa, rather than thinking of these urban spaces as separated from wild rural environ­ ments, says Young. De Oliveira stresses that, although hanta­ viruses are unlikely to cause large human outbreaks — because of the biology of the virus — funding cuts for global health pose challenges. There is now a “big lack of global health funding,” he says, with the US and many Euro­ pean countries “running out of money for global health because of other priorities such as defence”. USA https://doi.org/ 10.1073/pnas.1404958111 (2014). 3. Doebeli, M., Jaque, E. C. & Ispolatov, Y. Commun. Biol. https://doi.org/10.1038/s42003-021-02021-4 (2021). 4. Henley, P. & Shyaka, A. Nat. Med. https://doi.org/10.1038/ s41591-024-03473-x (2025).

papers.title: Hantavirus: biology, immune responses, and pathogenesis
papers.abstract: Abstract The recent Andes virus (ANDV) outbreak on the MV Hondius cruise has raised global public health alarms due to its dangerous ability to person-to-person spread. Hantavirus infections primarily manifest as hemorrhagic fever with Eurasian renal syndrome (HFRS) and Americas hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), both characterized by endothelial manifestation. Two principal mechanisms, virus-mediated cytopathy and host-driven immunopathology, have been proposed to account for the pathological progression, while their interplay is yet to be fully explored. In this review, we synthesize the recent research on hantavirus biology, cellular entry mechanisms, and epidemiological characteristics, and particularly highlight that viral immune evasion and subsequent uncontrolled host immune responses act as the core pathogenic drivers. Hantaviruses employ diverse strategies to antagonize type I interferon signaling and autophagy, which delay early innate immune activation and enable extensive viral dissemination. The excessive activation of cytotoxic CD8+ T cells, natural killer (NK) cells, combined with functionally impaired regulatory T cells and dysregulated humoral immunity, initiates severe inflammatory cascades, which in turn disrupt endothelial barrier integrity and cause organ vasculopathy. We also outline current therapeutic and preventive strategies, along with key directions for future research. A better understanding of hantavirus immunopathogenesis will help develop improved countermeasures against this zoonotic disease.

Cell Death and Disease https://doi.org/10.1038/s41419-026-09235-6 Introduction: the central paradox of hantavirus pathogenesis Hantaviruses present a classic paradigm in emerging infectious disease biology, where the central mechanistic puzzle remains fundamentally unresolved: how does a pathogen that establishes persistent, asymptomatic infection in its natural rodent reservoirs trigger severe, frequently lethal immunopathology upon spillover into accidental human hosts [1]? This biological dichotomy sits at the critical intersection of viral molecular biology, host-endothelial dynamics, and immunopathogenesis—domains that have generated competing explanatory frameworks over four decades of research [1, 2]. The two clinically distinct manifestations—hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in Eurasia and han- tavirus cardiopulmonary/pulmonary syndrome (HCPS/HPS) in the Americas—share an underlying mechanism of endothelial barrier disruption, yet diverge in target organ tropism and severity profiles [1, 2]. The field has oscillated between two dominant explanatory paradigms: a virus-centric model emphasizing direct cytopathic effects and a host-centric model foregrounding immune-mediated vascular damage. Contemporary evi- dence increasingly favors a synthesis in which viral immune evasion strategies paradoxically amplify subsequent immunopathology, but the precise mechanistic architecture of this interplay remains contested [3–5]. The urgency of resolving these contested mechanistic details has been underscored by an atypical, high-profile outbreak in May 2026 aboard the cruise ship MV Hondius [6]. This cluster, rapidly traced to Andes virus (ANDV) infection, has renewed focus on the unique biological features of New World hantaviruses—particularly their capacity for person-to-person transmission within closed environments [6, 7]. Accidental exposure of the human vascular network to aerosolized excreta from these specific reservoirs determines whether pathology shifts toward Eurasia-centric renal damage or Americas-centric cardiopulmonary syndrome. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41419-026-09235-6 Article in Press Cell Death and Disease Here, we synthesize the current scientific literature to map the evolving research landscape on hantaviruses across six key interconnected domains: viral biology and molecular structure, mechanisms of cellular entry and infection, innate and adaptive immune responses, pathogenic mechanisms of vascular leakage, global epidemiological trends, and emerging therapeutic and prophylactic strategies. Viral biology: molecular architecture and evolutionary constraints Genomic organization and structural determinants Hantaviruses are enveloped negative-sense single-stranded RNA viruses within the Hantaviridae family of the order Bunyavirales [4, 8, 9]. The genome contains three segments: the large (L) segment for RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), the medium (M) segment for glycoprotein precursor (GPC, cleaved co-translationally into envelope glycoproteins Gn and Gc), and the small (S) segment for nucleocapsid protein (NP)(Fig.1A). This tripartite segmented architecture permits genetic reassortment, conferring evolutionary flexibility that may generate viral variants with novel pathogenic properties [10]. The glycoproteins Gn and Gc are critical determinants of host cell tropism and are the primary targets for neutralizing antibody responses (Figs. 1B – D) [11, 12]. The M segment thus occupies a central position in pathogenicity determination: it encodes the molecules responsible for cellular attachment, membrane fusion, and the principal neutralization epitopes. Point mutations in glycoprotein sequences can profoundly alter viral infectivity, as demonstrated by studies showing that two amino acid substitutions in Old World hantavirus glycoproteins are sufficient to generate highly infectious recombinant vectors [13]. The evolutionary stability of these segments is illustrated by real-time genomic sequencing from the May 2026 MV Hondius outbreak cluster. Genomic sequencing and characterisation complemented the epidemiological investigation into the point of origin and subsequent transmission [14]. Each of the S, M, and L genomic segments from the three hantavirus isolates displays high sequence consistency. This observation suggests that the virus has not undergone reassortment, an evolutionary event in which segmented viral strains swap genetic fragments to generate new variants. Accordingly, the virus linked to this outbreak most probably originates from a single genetically stable lineage, instead of arising from recent genetic recombination between distinct hantavirus strains [14]. The RdRp and cap-snatching mechanism The L segment-encoded RdRp mediates both transcription and replication. A distinctive feature of hantavirus mRNA synthesis is the cap-snatching mechanism, whereby the viral RdRp cleaves short capped RNA primers from mRNAs of host origin to initiate viral transcription. This process requires host cell factors, establishing a fundamental dependency on the cellular transcriptional machinery [15]. This host factor requirement for cap snatching represents a potential therapeutic vulnerability, as disruption of this interaction could selectively inhibit viral replication without directly targeting host processes. Host reservoir biology and spillover dynamics Each hantavirus species has co-evolved with a specific rodent host reservoir in which persistent, asymptomatic infection is maintained (Table 1) [16]. The striped field mouse (Apodemus agrarius) serves as the main natural reservoir host of Hantaan virus (HTNV). In European regions, bank voles (Myodes glareolus) act as persistent carriers that preserve Puumala virus (PUUV) [16]. The ANDV virus is carried by Oligoryzomys longicaudatus, a wild rodent commonly called the long-tailed colilargo. The geographical range of this species extends from northern Chile and northwestern Argentina where there is a stable population. This rodent is not naturally present in Europe and in the United States, and established wild Article in Press https://doi.org/10.1038/s41419-026-09235-6 Cell Death and Disease populations of this species are completely absent abroad. This is crucial since introduction to local rodent populations and potential subsequent rodent-to-human transmission in Europe is not expected [16]. Human infection is accidental, occurring primarily through inhalation of aerosolized virus-containing rodent excreta (urine, feces, saliva) [4, 16]. The mechanisms by which reservoir hosts suppress pathology while maintaining viremia—likely involving regulatory T cell-mediated immunosuppression—stand in stark contrast to the hyperin- flammatory response in humans [3, 11]. Understanding this dichotomy remains one of the field’s central theoretical challenges. Sustained human-to-human transmission has been validated only for ANDV among hantavirus species [7, 17]. The outbreak on the MV Hondius is considered a case study of a potential superspreader scenario, allowing the effects of prolonged case contact, closed ventilation, delayed symptom appearance and late diagnosis to be studied in a real-life context. All conditions were present to allow secondary cases aboard the ship and tertiary cases across international borders [7]. Mechanisms of cellular entry and tropism Receptor utilization and endothelial tropism Hantaviruses preferentially target endothelial cells, which constitutes the mechanistic basis for the vascular pathology that defines both HFRS and HCPS [4]. The primary cellular receptors for pathogenic hantaviruses include αvβ3 integrin for pathogenic strains, and αvβ1 integrin for non-pathogenic strains, and latest work identifies PCDH1 as a key receptor governing the cellular entry of New World hantaviruses [18]. This receptor specificity provides a molecular explanation for endothelial tropism and suggests that the tropism itself—rather than any direct cytopathic mechanism—positions the virus to trigger vascular dysfunction through immune-mediated collateral damage (Fig. 2). Non-lytic infection and its pathogenic implications A critical distinguishing feature of hantavirus biology is that infection of endothelial cells is non-cytopathic [19]. Unlike many hemorrhagic fever viruses that destroy target cells directly, hantaviruses establish productive infection without inducing overt cellular damage. This non-lytic character has profound implications for pathogenesis theory: it necessarily redirects pathogenic mechanisms toward indirect, immune-mediated injury rather than direct viral cytopathology (Fig. 2). Furthermore, hantaviruses actively inhibit apoptosis in infected cells, promoting viral per- sistence and potentially amplifying subsequent immune-mediated damage when cytotoxic responses eventually target infected endothelium [20]. Fig. 2 Mechanisms of cellular entry and tropism. Schematic depicting hantavirus infection of endothelial cells. Receptor specificity (αvβ3, αvβ1, and PCDH1) drives endothelial tropism. Infection is non-lytic, with viral inhibition of apoptosis promoting persistence. Pathogenesis arises from indirect, immune-mediated endothelial activation and vascular dysfunction, rather than direct cytopathology. (Created in https://BioRender.com). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41419-026-09235-6 Article in Press Cell Death and Disease Immune responses: the double-edged sword Hantavirus immunopathogenesis is driven by viral immune evasion and subsequent host immune dysregulation. Suppression of type I interferon signaling by the virus promotes systemic dissemination. Together with regulatory T cell deficiency and hyperactivation of CD8+ T cells, NK cells, and B cells, these cells elicit exaggerated cytotoxic responses, which ultimately cause endothelial damage, complement activation and vascular leakage in severe infections (Fig. 3). Innate immune activation and viral evasion Hantaviruses have evolved sophisticated mechanisms to evade and delay innate immune detection, particularly the type I interferon (IFN-I) response [21]. The IFN-I signaling pathway, mediated through RIG-I-like receptors (RLRs), is the primary cellular sensor for hantavirus RNA. However, multiple viral proteins actively antagonize this pathway: the glycoprotein cytoplasmic tail inhibits TRAF3/TBK1-directed IRF3 activation, while the nucleocapsid protein (NP) sequesters double-stranded RNA intermediates to prevent RLR activation [22]. Recent work has identified TRIM25 as a specific target of Hantaan virus immune evasion. HTNV inhibits the type I interferon response by targeting RLR signaling pathways through TRIM25 [21]. Furthermore, the glycoprotein and Fig. 3 Immune evasion and immunopathogenesis of hantavirus infection. Hantaviruses enter endothelial cells and replicate with limited cytopathic effect. Early antagonism of type I interferon responses may delay innate immune activation and facilitate viral dissemination. Persistent infection, insufficient immune regulation, exaggerated CD8+/NK cell responses, and complement activation converge to disrupt endothelial barrier integrity, leading to vascular leakage and organ failure. Article in Press https://doi.org/10.1038/s41419-026-09235-6 Cell Death and Disease nucleocapsid protein encoded by hantaviruses modulate autophagic flux to suppress the host’s innate immune reactions [23]. By disrupting normal autophagic signaling, these viral proteins suppress IFN-I production and inflammatory cytokine secretion, creating a permissive environment for early viral replication. The theoretical significance of these evasion strategies extends beyond mere immune escape. By delaying the initial innate response, hantaviruses allow greater viral dissemination before adaptive immunity is engaged. When the adaptive response finally mounts, it confronts a more widely distributed infection, necessitating a more vigorous effector response—one that, in the context of endothelial tropism, inevitably causes collateral vascular damage. This “delay-and-amplify” model represents the current leading framework for understanding hantavirus immunopatho- genesis [3, 5]. Mononuclear phagocyte redistribution A marked redistribution of peripheral mononuclear phagocytes (MNPs) to the airways occurs during acute Puumala virus (PUUV) infection, which likely drives localized immune activation at the initial infection focus [3]. Pathogenic hantaviruses can replicate within cells of the mononuclear phagocyte system (MPS), and this replication capacity has been proposed as a determinant of pathogenicity [24]. The ability to productively infect and disseminate through MPS cells may explain systemic viral spread and the multi-organ involvement characteristic of severe hantavirus disease. Cytotoxic lymphocyte responses: CD8+ T cells and NK cells The adaptive immune response to hantavirus infection is dominated by a vigorous cytotoxic lymphocyte response involving both CD8+ T and NK cells. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) studies in patients with acute PUUV infection have revealed increased numbers of activated CD8+ T and NK cells, along with elevated granzyme A and granzyme B [25]. papers.title: Angiopoietin-1/Tie2 Activation as a Therapeutic Hypothesis for Hantavirus-Induced Vascular Permeability
papers.abstract: Severe hantavirus infection produces extensive vascular leakage, driven by a combination of endothelial dysfunction, dysregulated inflammation, VEGF-mediated hyperpermeability, angiopoietin imbalance, and degradation of the endothelial glycocalyx. This narrative review draws on the peer-reviewed literature, with particular attention to work published between 2016 and 2026, to examine how hantavirus-induced vascular permeability arises in hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), and how Angiopoietin-1 (Ang-1)/Tie2 signaling and glycocalyx injury contribute to endothelial barrier failure. Direct hantavirus evidence shows that Ang-1 inhibits hantavirus-directed endothelial permeability in vitro and that angiopoietin dysregulation tracks with disease severity in patients; findings that Tie2 activation curbs vascular leakage in sepsis and other non-hantavirus models are mechanistically suggestive but remain inferential rather than hantavirus-specific. No hantavirus animal model or clinical trial has yet evaluated Ang-1/Tie2-directed therapy, so this review treats the approach as a testable hypothesis rather than an established or recommended treatment; confirming its therapeutic value will require dedicated hantavirus-specific animal and clinical studies.
